title: Compact Symmetric Spaces: Weyl Alcoves And Rank-One Geometry
notes: Open by contrasting this chapter with the noncompact story from the previous unit. The Lie algebra splitting is still the local engine, but compactness makes geodesics return, makes the exponential map fold, and forces students to replace one global coordinate chart by a controlled collection of Weyl chambers, lattice translations, and rank-one models.

title: What Replaces The Noncompact Polar Chart?
notes: Use this slide to name the central replacement. In noncompact type the exponential coordinates on p are globally clean. In compact type that same map is periodic and singular along predictable walls. The point of the chapter is not a collection of isolated facts; it is a diagrammatic machine for deciding when two flat directions represent the same geometric point and where geodesic coordinates fail.

title: The Compact Exponential Map Folds
notes: A sphere is the friendliest model for the global change. Near the base point, geodesic coordinates behave just as expected. At the antipodal level, angular Jacobi fields collapse and the exponential map stops being a coordinate chart. Tell students to keep this simple sine factor in mind, because the higher-rank chapter repeats it root by root rather than only radially.

title: Reduce The Geometry To A Maximal Flat
notes: This slide should make maximal flats feel like a deliberate compression rather than a loss of information. The isotropy group moves many tangent vectors into a chosen a, and regular points in a avoid all root walls. Once students accept this reduction, the rest of the chapter becomes a study of how the finite and affine reflection groups carve this flat into meaningful regions.

title: Weyl Groups Identify Equivalent Directions
notes: Define the Weyl group as a quotient of a normalizer by a centralizer, but immediately translate that quotient into a geometric action on the flat. A regular geodesic direction does not care which chamber copy we happened to draw. The finite Weyl group is the first layer of redundancy, and its chamber picture is the finite part of the later affine alcove tiling.

title: Conjugate Points Sit On Affine Root Walls
notes: The key teaching move is to separate two meanings of a wall. A wall through the origin says a direction has extra symmetry and is singular. A translated wall says the exponential map has moved far enough along a regular direction for a root Jacobi factor to vanish. Students should see that the same root system controls both phenomena, but with different offsets.

title: Regular Points Are The Interior Of The Diagram
notes: Pause here because students often merge singular and conjugate into one vague idea. A singular direction has extra centralizer at the point of departure or along a wall through the origin. A conjugate point is about the differential of the exponential map losing rank after travel. The diagram lets us compare these conditions without pretending they are the same condition.

title: Compact Groups Add Lattice And Center Data
notes: This is the chapter's reminder that Lie algebra data alone does not specify every compact global form. A maximal torus makes periodic directions visible, the unit lattice says when exponentials return to the identity, and the center determines possible quotients. Keep the language concrete: the same local symmetric-pair geometry can lead to different globally compact spaces.

title: The Affine Weyl Group Tiles The Flat
notes: Now assemble the finite and periodic information. The finite Weyl group alone folds a neighborhood of the origin, but compact geodesics also return after lattice translations. The affine Weyl group combines both operations. A closed alcove is not just a pretty triangle; it is the chosen coordinate domain after all the finite reflection and periodic identifications have been accounted for.

title: An Alcove Is A System Of Inequalities
notes: Make the affine picture computational. A student should be able to test a sample point by checking nonnegative simple-root coordinates and the highest-root bound. In the A2 normalization, the highest root is alpha1 plus alpha2, so the slanted wall is the first place the compact domain closes. This is also the lab pattern used by the notebook.

title: Locally Isometric Spaces Need Global Quotient Data
notes: This slide is about avoiding a local-to-global mistake. Curvature and infinitesimal symmetric-pair data identify the local geometry, but compact spaces may still differ by central quotient choices. The diagram on the right is not a theorem proof; it is a bookkeeping map showing where universal covers, centers, candidate isotropy subgroups, and final quotient diagrams enter.

title: Rank-One Compact Spaces Are The Test Cases
notes: Rank-one spaces are the sanity checks for the whole chapter. There is only one flat direction up to isotropy, so the diagram collapses to intervals and endpoint behavior. Spheres make the antipodal point visible, while projective and complex or quaternionic examples turn the endpoint into a higher-dimensional midpoint or cut locus. These examples keep the algebraic alcove language tied to geometry.

title: Shortest Closed Geodesics See The First Wall
notes: Students may expect compact geodesics to be periodic and minimizing for the same reason, but those are different thresholds. The first wall is the cut or conjugate warning, while the full lattice period records closure. In rank one the distinction is easy to draw on a line. In higher rank, root directions decide which wall arrives first.

title: Small Singular Sets Do Not Derail Global Arguments
notes: Treat this appendix as a safety net for the chapter's global arguments. Singular sets are not ignored because they are unimportant. They are controlled because their dimension is low enough that generic paths and sometimes homotopies can avoid them. This explains why arguments can work on the regular part and then extend to the compact space with carefully stated exceptions.

title: Classify Points In A Compact Flat
notes: This applied slide turns the previous theory into a classroom exercise. Give students a point in simple-root coordinates and ask them to classify it before discussing the geometry. The important habit is not the A2 numbers themselves; it is the translation from geometric language into wall inequalities and then back into statements about regularity, conjugacy, and quotient representatives.

title: How The Chapter's Arguments Tend To Move
notes: This is the synthesis slide before the final checklist. It gives students a way to read dense theorem statements without losing the plot. First put everything in a maximal flat. Then let roots cut the flat. Then quotient by finite and affine Weyl symmetries. Finally bring back the center and quotient information needed for the actual compact space. That four-step route explains many proofs in the chapter.

title: Compact Type Checklist
notes: Close by returning to the chapter's central replacement: a compact symmetric space is understood through flats, roots, chambers, affine identifications, and quotient data. Students should leave with a concrete workflow rather than a pile of definitions. If they can classify a point in the alcove, explain why the exponential map folds, and name where center data enters, they have the core of the chapter.
